questions.stem: Who is known as the 'FATHER OF GENETICS', and on which plant did he perform his classic experiments between 1856-1863?
questions.explanation: GREGOR JOHANN MENDEL (1822-1884), an Augustinian friar in Brünn (Brno), Moravia (now Czech Republic), conducted experiments on the GARDEN PEA PLANT (Pisum sativum) in the monastery garden. Published his results in 1866 ('Versuche über Pflanzenhybriden' — Experiments on Plant Hybridisation) — but they were IGNORED for 35 YEARS. Rediscovered independently in 1900 by three scientists: HUGO DE VRIES (Netherlands), CARL CORRECTENS (Germany), ERICH VON TSCHERMAK (Austria). Mendel chose PEAS because: (a) easy self-pollination (bisexual flowers); (b) clear contrasting traits (7 pairs — tall/dwarf, round/wrinkled, yellow/green seeds, etc.); (c) short generation time. THOMAS HUNT MORGAN (Nobel 1933) worked on Drosophila (fruit fly) and established chromosomal theory.

questions.stem: Mendel's THREE laws of inheritance are:

options.option_text: Law of Dominance, Law of Segregation, Law of Independent Assortment
Law of Conservation, Law of Mutation, Law of Natural Selection
Law of Variation, Law of Similarity, Law of Mutability
Law of Descent, Law of Progress, Law of Succession

questions.explanation: Mendel's THREE LAWS: (1) LAW OF DOMINANCE — in a pair of contrasting traits, the dominant trait masks the recessive in F1. (E.g., Tt = Tall because T dominates t.) (2) LAW OF SEGREGATION — during gamete formation, the two alleles of a gene SEPARATE (segregate) so each gamete carries only one. (Cell mechanism: meiosis I.) Also called the 'LAW OF PURITY OF GAMETES'. (3) LAW OF INDEPENDENT ASSORTMENT — during formation of gametes, alleles of different genes assort INDEPENDENTLY (only true for genes on different chromosomes or far apart on same chromosome). Produces dihybrid ratios of 9:3:3:1 in F2. Modern exceptions: Incomplete dominance (RR × rr → Rr pink), codominance (AB blood group), multiple alleles (blood type), epistasis, linkage (genes on same chromosome), sex-linkage, polygenic inheritance.

questions.stem: In a monohybrid cross of pure-breeding tall (TT) × pure-breeding dwarf (tt) pea plants, what is the PHENOTYPIC ratio observed in the F2 generation?
questions.explanation: MONOHYBRID CROSS: P: TT × tt → F1: all Tt (tall, heterozygous). F1 × F1 (Tt × Tt) → F2 genotypes: 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt = 1:2:1 GENOTYPIC ratio. PHENOTYPIC: 3 Tall (TT + 2Tt both show dominant allele) : 1 Dwarf (tt only). For DIHYBRID CROSS (two traits, e.g., seed shape × colour): TTYY × ttyy → F1 all TtYy → F2 shows 9 T_Y_ : 3 T_yy : 3 ttY_ : 1 ttyy = 9:3:3:1 phenotypic. Also: TEST CROSS = cross with recessive homozygote (tt). If unknown × tt = all tall → unknown was TT. If 1:1 → Tt. BACK CROSS = cross with either parent.

questions.stem: DNA's double-helix structure was elucidated in 1953 by James Watson and Francis Crick using X-ray diffraction data from:
questions.explanation: ROSALIND FRANKLIN (1920-1958) — crystallographer at King's College London — took the famous 'PHOTO 51' (X-ray diffraction of DNA fibre, 1952), which clearly showed the helical structure. Her colleague MAURICE WILKINS showed the photo (WITHOUT her permission) to Watson + Crick, who combined it with Chargaff's base-pairing rules to publish the DOUBLE-HELIX model in Nature (25 April 1953). NOBEL PRIZE 1962: Watson + Crick + Wilkins (Franklin had died of ovarian cancer in 1958 — Nobels are not awarded posthumously). Widely considered an injustice; Franklin's role was under-recognised for decades. ERWIN CHARGAFF's rules (1950): A=T, G=C in any DNA (base-pairing implication). OSWALD AVERY et al. (1944) proved DNA (not protein) is the genetic material using Streptococcus pneumoniae (Avery-MacLeod-McCarty experiment). and Maurice Wilkins.

questions.stem: A normal human somatic (body) cell has how many chromosomes, and how are they organised?

options.option_text: 46 chromosomes (23 PAIRS — 22 autosomal pairs + 1 pair of sex chromosomes)

questions.explanation: Humans have 46 CHROMOSOMES (23 pairs): 22 pairs of AUTOSOMES (numbered 1-22 by size; 1 is largest, 21 smallest; wait — actually 22 is smallest but chromosome 21 was numbered before size correction — historical anomaly) + 1 pair of SEX CHROMOSOMES (XX female or XY male). KARYOTYPE: 46,XX (female) or 46,XY (male). GAMETES (egg/sperm) are HAPLOID (n=23). Zygote = diploid (2n=46). Chromosomal abnormalities: DOWN SYNDROME (trisomy 21 — 47 chromosomes), KLINEFELTER (XXY, 47), TURNER (XO, 45), EDWARDS (trisomy 18), PATAU (trisomy 13). Interesting: chimpanzees + other great apes have 48 (24 pairs); human chromosome 2 is a fusion of two ancestral ape chromosomes. Chromosome 1 has ~8% of genome; Y is the smallest + gene-poor.

options.option_text: Point mutation in a single gene

questions.explanation: DOWN SYNDROME = TRISOMY 21 — three copies of chromosome 21 (total 47 chromosomes; 47,XX or 47,XY,+21). First described by JOHN LANGDON DOWN (British physician, 1866); cause identified by JÉRÔME LEJEUNE (French, 1959). Causes: (1) 95% cases — NONDISJUNCTION during maternal meiosis (risk rises with maternal age: 1 in 1500 at age 25, 1 in 100 at age 40); (2) 4% — ROBERTSONIAN TRANSLOCATION of chr 21 onto another acrocentric (14, 15, 21, 22); (3) 1% — MOSAIC (some cells trisomic, others normal). Features: intellectual disability (mild-moderate), characteristic facial features (flat nasal bridge, upward slanting eyes, epicanthal folds), single palmar crease, heart defects (~50%), increased Alzheimer risk. Other well-known aneuploidies: TURNER (45,X — female, short stature, sterile), KLINEFELTER (47,XXY — male, small testes, gynecomastia), PATAU (47,+13), EDWARDS (47,+18). three copies instead of two.

questions.stem: HAEMOPHILIA and COLOUR BLINDNESS are examples of:
questions.explanation: X-LINKED RECESSIVE disorders: mutation on X chromosome; one X + one Y in males means a single recessive X allele manifests (no 'second X' to mask it). Famous examples: HAEMOPHILIA A (Factor VIII deficiency — 'Royal disease' — Queen Victoria was a carrier, passed to European royal families including Russian Tsarevich Alexei); HAEMOPHILIA B (Christmas disease, Factor IX); COLOUR BLINDNESS (red-green, 8% of men vs 0.5% of women); DUCHENNE MUSCULAR DYSTROPHY (dystrophin gene); G6PD deficiency. Pattern: affected FATHER × carrier MOTHER → daughters 50% carriers, 50% affected; sons 50% affected. If healthy father × carrier mother → daughters 50% carrier; sons 50% affected. AUTOSOMAL DOMINANT: Huntington's, Marfan, achondroplasia. AUTOSOMAL RECESSIVE: cystic fibrosis, sickle cell, thalassemia, PKU. Y-LINKED: rare, affects males only, father→son (e.g., some forms of male infertility).

questions.stem: SICKLE CELL ANAEMIA is caused by a point mutation in which gene, and the result is:

options.option_text: β-globin gene (HBB): Glutamate → Valine at position 6

questions.explanation: SICKLE CELL ANAEMIA: single-point missense mutation GAG → GTG in the β-globin gene (HBB, chromosome 11), changing GLUTAMATE (E/Glu) → VALINE (V/Val) at position 6 of the β chain. Produces abnormal HbS hemoglobin. Under low O₂ conditions, HbS polymerises, distorting RBCs into SICKLE shape → block capillaries (vaso-occlusive crises) → pain, stroke, organ damage. Inheritance: AUTOSOMAL RECESSIVE. HETEROZYGOTES (HbA/HbS — sickle cell TRAIT) are largely asymptomatic AND have RESISTANCE TO MALARIA (heterozygote advantage — classic example of BALANCED POLYMORPHISM). This explains high sickle-cell prevalence in malarial regions (sub-Saharan Africa, parts of India). Discovered by Linus Pauling (1949) as the FIRST MOLECULAR DISEASE — showed the link between gene mutation and protein defect. Treatment: hydroxyurea; bone marrow transplant; recent CRISPR-based gene therapies (Casgevy approved 2023).

questions.stem: The HUMAN GENOME PROJECT (HGP) — which sequenced the entire human genome — was officially declared complete in:
questions.explanation: HUMAN GENOME PROJECT timeline: LAUNCHED 1990 by NIH + DOE (US); Francis Collins later directed. Initial draft: 2000 (joint White House announcement by Clinton, Blair, Collins + Craig Venter of private Celera). DECLARED COMPLETE: April 14, 2003 — 50th anniversary of Watson-Crick DNA structure paper. Covered ~92% of euchromatic genome. COST: ~$2.7 billion. TIME: 13 years. Key findings: ~20,000-25,000 protein-coding genes (much fewer than expected 100,000); only ~1-2% of genome codes for proteins; the rest is regulatory, repetitive (transposons), or non-coding. COMPLETE 100% finally achieved by T2T (Telomere-to-Telomere) Consortium in 2022 using long-read sequencing. Indian's contribution: CSIR-IGIB's IndiGen project (2019+). Today NGS (next-gen sequencing) can sequence a human genome in ~1 day for under $1000. 50th anniversary of DNA structure discovery.
